group.title: Formal and legal English
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Information heard from others that cannot be directly proved, usually not accepted as evidence.
examples: The judge refused to accept {hearsay} about what the neighbor had said.
wrong: The video was hearsay, since everyone could see exactly what happened.

words.meaning: A wrong that causes harm to someone and lets them claim money in a civil court.
examples: Negligent driving can be a {tort} as well as a crime.
wrong: A tort is a kind of contract both sides sign happily.

words.meaning: A written statement someone swears is true, used as evidence.
examples: The witness signed an {affidavit} before a notary.
wrong: An affidavit is a spoken rumor that nobody swears to.

words.meaning: A court order that tells someone to do or stop doing something.
examples: The court issued an {injunction} to halt the construction.
wrong: The injunction allowed the company to keep doing whatever it liked.

words.meaning: A court decision that a person is not guilty.
examples: The jury’s {acquittal} meant he walked free.
wrong: After his acquittal, he was taken to prison to serve his sentence.

words.meaning: A formal charge that someone has committed a serious crime; also strong criticism.
examples: The grand jury returned an {indictment} against the mayor.
wrong: The indictment declared him completely innocent of any crime.

words.meaning: To promise to pay for any loss or damage another person may suffer.
examples: The contract {indemnifies} the landlord against tenant damage.
wrong: The insurer indemnified us, so we had to pay for all the damage ourselves.

words.meaning: The official legal process of proving a will is valid and sharing out a dead person’s property.
examples: The house can’t be sold until {probate} is complete.
wrong: Probate is the process of writing a will while you are young and healthy.

words.meaning: By means of this statement or document.
examples: I {hereby} resign from my position.
wrong: I hereby resign, said the letter that was never written.

words.meaning: Until now; before this time.
examples: The rule applies to all cases {heretofore} decided.
wrong: Heretofore refers only to things that will happen in the future.

words.meaning: In agreement with or as required by a law, rule or agreement.
examples: The goods were returned {pursuant to} the terms of the contract.
wrong: They acted pursuant to the contract by ignoring every term in it.

words.meaning: Having no legal force at all.
examples: The agreement was declared {null and void}.
wrong: The contract is null and void, so both sides must follow every clause.

words.meaning: Honestly and with sincere intentions.
examples: Both sides negotiated {in good faith}.
wrong: He acted in good faith by secretly lying to his partners.

words.meaning: To have a document signed and stamped by an official to show it is genuine.
examples: You must {notarize} the contract before the bank will accept it.
wrong: She notarized the letter so that no official would ever check it.

words.meaning: A legal claim or debt attached to property that limits what the owner can do with it.
examples: The house was sold free of any {encumbrance}, so the buyer owed nothing.
wrong: An encumbrance on the land means the owner may sell it with no limits at all.

words.meaning: Settling a dispute by letting a neutral person decide, instead of going to court.
examples: The contract requires {arbitration} for any disagreement.
wrong: They chose arbitration, so no outside person was involved in deciding.

words.meaning: To make an official decision about a dispute or claim.
examples: A panel of judges will {adjudicate} the case.
wrong: The judge adjudicated the case by refusing to make any decision.

words.meaning: To officially end or cancel a law, treaty or agreement.
examples: The new government {abrogated} the old treaty.
wrong: They abrogated the treaty by signing it and keeping it in force.

words.meaning: That must legally be obeyed.
examples: The ruling is final and {binding}.
wrong: The contract is binding, so either side can ignore it freely.

words.meaning: That can be made to work by law.
examples: A spoken promise is not always {enforceable}.
wrong: The rule was enforceable, so no court could ever apply it.

words.meaning: The exact words of a law rather than its general purpose.
examples: She followed {the letter of the law} but ignored its spirit.
wrong: Following the letter of the law means breaking its exact wording.

words.meaning: A serious crime, such as robbery or murder, that carries a heavy punishment.
examples: Armed robbery is a {felony} in every state.
wrong: Dropping litter is a felony that can bring a life sentence.

words.meaning: A minor crime that is less serious than a felony.
examples: Shoplifting a small item is usually a {misdemeanor}.
wrong: Murder is the classic example of a misdemeanor.

words.meaning: A law that sets a time limit after which a case can no longer be brought.
examples: The claim failed because the {statute of limitations} had run out.
wrong: The statute of limitations lets you file a claim at any time, forever.

words.meaning: An official addition that changes part of a will.
examples: She added a {codicil} leaving her paintings to the museum.
wrong: A codicil is the original will itself, written for the first time.

words.meaning: To leave money or property to someone in a will.
examples: He {bequeathed} his library to the university.
wrong: She bequeathed the house to her nephew while she was buying it.

words.meaning: A condition added to an agreement.
examples: He accepted, with the {proviso} that he could work from home.
wrong: The proviso meant the deal had no conditions at all.

words.meaning: A deal in which an accused person admits a lesser crime in return for a lighter sentence.
examples: He took a {plea bargain} and avoided a long trial.
wrong: With a plea bargain, the accused denies everything and asks for a harsher sentence.

words.meaning: Relating to a higher court that hears appeals.
examples: The {appellate} court overturned the earlier decision.
wrong: An appellate court is the first court that ever hears a case.

words.meaning: To step back from a case because you might not be fair.
examples: The judge {recused} herself because she knew the defendant.
wrong: He recused himself, so he went on to decide the case alone.

words.meaning: Involving trust, especially a duty to act in another person’s financial interest.
examples: Trustees have a {fiduciary} duty to protect the fund.
wrong: His fiduciary duty allowed him to use clients’ money for himself.

words.meaning: A formal written promise or agreement, often in a contract or deed.
examples: A {covenant} in the deed forbids building a second house.
wrong: A covenant is a casual remark with no promise in it.

words.meaning: A legal right to keep or sell someone’s property until a debt is paid.
examples: The builder put a {lien} on the house for unpaid work.
wrong: A lien gives a lender no claim to the property at all.

words.meaning: A special court or official body that judges certain kinds of disputes.
examples: Her case went to an employment {tribunal}.
wrong: A tribunal is a party where nobody makes any decisions.

words.meaning: Sworn evidence given outside court and recorded for later use.
examples: Her {deposition} was taken in the lawyer’s office.
wrong: A deposition is evidence nobody records or swears to.

words.meaning: Mercy, especially a decision to reduce a punishment.
examples: The governor granted {clemency} to the elderly prisoner.
wrong: Showing clemency, the judge doubled the sentence.

words.meaning: To announce a new law or rule officially; to spread an idea widely.
examples: New safety rules were {promulgated} last month.
wrong: The government promulgated the law by keeping it secret.

words.meaning: The theory and study of law, or a body of legal decisions.
examples: Her book is a classic of modern {jurisprudence}.
wrong: Jurisprudence is the study of how to bake bread.

words.meaning: Wrong or illegal conduct, especially by an official.
examples: The director was fired for financial {malfeasance}.
wrong: She was praised for her malfeasance, her perfectly honest work.

words.meaning: A legal right requiring that a held person be brought before a court to check their detention is lawful.
examples: The lawyer filed for {habeas corpus} to free her client.
wrong: Habeas corpus lets the state hold people forever without any court hearing.
